STFSDM also decreased the root mean square error of simulated SD by 2.82% and 15.82%, compared to two local parameter optimization experiments that only utilized air temperature or ground surface temperature. These results showed that STFSDM increased estimated fresh snow density and thus reduced SD overestimation by considering ground surface temperature, and achieved more accurate SD simulationbecause it incorporated two distinct temperature-driven effects on fresh snow density: (1) the influence of air temperature on ice crystal formation as ice crystals fall, and (2) the impact of surface temperature on snow compaction upon landing. Thus, STFSDM reduces simulated SD overestimation under the observational conditions of QTP meteorological stations. This scheme is most applicable to SD simulations in areas similar to the QTP with short-duration seasonal snow cover.

title: Do CMIP6 models reduce the uncertainty in sub-daily extreme precipitation projections?
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Archana Majhi, Sonali Pattanayak, C.T. Dhanya, Sumedha Chakma
abstract: The significant advancement in climate modeling has encouraged the scientific community to use updated projections such as CMIP6 with the expectations of better reliability as compared to its predecessor, CMIP5. The question, however, is whether these improvements have reduced the uncertainty in the projected sub-daily extreme precipitation at global scales, and if yes, how much. This question is addressed through the quantification of uncertainty using a mutual information-based weighted variance method and the comparative analysis of uncertainty in their probability distributions across quartiles, latitudinal profiles, and uncertainty risk maps derived from CMIP5 and CMIP6 GCMs. Comparing their quartile ranges showed that CMIP6 ensemble has lower uncertainty than CMIP5. The CMIP6 uncertainty risk map demonstrated a substantial increase in low uncertainty areas and a decline in hotspot areas for the Simple Hourly-Precipitation Intensity Index, Wet Spell Length, and Annual Total Precipitation indices, but there was a marked increase in hotspot regions for Monthly MAXimum 3Hourly-precipitation (MAX3H). The MAX3H have increased uncertainty particularly in West and East Africa, Southeast Asia, Amazon, and Northern Australian regions contributing 16 – 22% of global land regions. Nevertheless, it exhibited a seasonal average reduction in uncertainty of 25 to 35%, whilst the other indices demonstrated a reduction of 35 to 50% over the global land regions. However, this study confirms that the CMIP6 models have successfully added further credibility to their future sub-daily precipitation projections. Additionally, the study suggests careful model evaluation against extreme precipitation especially for tropics and improvement in the representation of vegetation and associated biogeochemical processes with deeper understanding of biases affecting land atmosphere coupling especially at dense vegetative areas.

title: A decentralized multi-agent framework for adaptive water allocation in river-reservoir systems
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Hossein Ghanaei, Mahta Nazari, Amirreza Tadayon, Reza Kerachian
abstract: Efficient surface water allocation in large river basins remains a significant challenge due to the presence of multiple stakeholders with conflicting objectives and limited coordination. Traditional centralized optimization approaches often fail to adequately represent stakeholder autonomy and are difficult to implement in practice. To address these limitations, this study proposes a decentralized, adaptive multi-agent water allocation model for river–reservoir systems, in which water users are explicitly represented as autonomous decision-making agents. The model introduces an adaptive and decentralized allocation framework that explicitly links long-term hydrological forecasting with constraint-based optimization and medium-term (one-year, monthly time-step) operating rules, thereby enabling dynamic water allocation under physical, operational, and environmental constraints. The allocation problem is formulated as a Distributed Constraint Optimization Problem (DCOP), allowing coordination without centralized control. Four DCOP algorithms—Maximum Gain Messaging (MGM), MGM2, Distributed Stochastic Algorithm (DSA), and Distributed Pseudo-tree Optimization Procedure (DPOP)—are evaluated based on allocation efficiency, cost deviation, and computational performance. An application to the Karkheh River Basin in Iran demonstrates that DPOP and DSA achieve allocation costs within 17.6% and 21.2% of the centralized benchmark, respectively, while simultaneously maintaining downstream water supply reliability, hydropower production targets, and environmental flow requirements. These results quantitatively confirm the model’s capability to balance efficiency, equity, and computational scalability, underscoring its suitability for real-world, decentralized water resources management.

title: Shifting flood regimes in Arctic basins under climate change
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Shanshan Hu, Zhiying Wang, Tingting Wang, Yifei Hua, Wenbin Liu
abstract: Global warming intensifies the hydrological cycle, increasing the frequency and magnitude of floods worldwide, a trend particularly pronounced in the Arctic, where enhanced flooding exacerbates erosion and impacts ecosystems. However, the key drivers of Arctic flood variability remain unclear. To address this, we integrated hydrological and statistical modelling to quantify the contributions of hydrological factors to flood changes across 13 major Arctic rivers. We first reconstructed daily discharge using the CemaNeige-GR4J model, which, through multi-objective calibration targeting both runoff and snow processes, performed robustly (total Kling–Gupta Efficiency > 0.7 in most basins) and significantly improved the simulation of snow dynamics. Our analysis reveals spatially heterogeneous trends: flood magnitudes (maximum daily discharge) increased significantly on annual and seasonal scales in most basins (0.33–1567.17 m3·s−1·yr−1), while flood timing (date of maximum discharge) shifted earlier in spring/summer and later in autumn. Critically, all-subsets regression attribution shows that for ∼70% of the basins, interannual flood variations are predominantly driven by antecedent moisture conditions—specifically, soil moisture and snow water equivalent—rather than by precipitation or snowmelt events. This finding underscores the dominant role of accumulated basin storage over short-term meteorological extremes in shaping Arctic flood regimes.

title: Satellite water quality monitoring of China’s coastal inland waters based on Google Earth Engine
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Yaqi Zhao, Yujia Yan, Xianqiang He, Zhiyan Chen, Teng Li, Xuchen Jin, Liu Zhao, Fang Gong, Fajun Jiang, Yan Bai
abstract: Monitoring water quality parameters (WQPs) in coastal inland waters remains challenging because pronounced spatiotemporal variability and complex pollutant sources limit the robustness of conventional retrieval methods. High-resolution Earth-observation satellites improve spatial detail for fine-scale monitoring, but their application over large-area is constrained by substantial computational demands. Moreover, in optically complex waters, spectral information alone is often insufficient, highlighting the need to incorporate geographic and environmental predictors into WQP retrieval models. In this study, we developed a Google Earth Engine (GEE)-based workflow to retrieve four management-relevant WQPs across China’s coastal inland waters: permanganate index (CODMn), total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), and turbidity (TUB). A large matched dataset was constructed by linking Sentinel-2 remote sensing reflectance (R rs) with observations from automatic monitoring-stations, as well as geographic and environmental covariates. Based on this dataset, lightweight multimodal machine-learning models were developed to integrate optical, spatial, and environmental predictors within a computationally efficient, scalable framework. The models showed good predictive performance, with validation R2 values of 0.759–0.827 and independent test R2 values of 0.664–0.734, indicating satisfactory accuracy and transferability. Application to 2024 imagery in China’s coastal inland waters revealed clear spatial gradients, with CODMn, TN, and TP generally higher in northern regions, particularly in estuarine and nearshore waters. Seasonal patterns showed summer–autumn maxima for CODMn, TP, and TUB, whereas TN peaked in winter–spring. The proposed GEE-based framework provides a practical and transferable approach for WQP monitoring and water-environment assessment.

title: A novel framework for Identifying and predicting stratified land deformation: a case study of the Beijing Plain
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Xiaoyu Chu, Beibei Chen, Ziyao Ma, Huili Gong, Chaofan Zhou, Xincheng Wang, Kunchao Lei, Haigang Wang
abstract: Regional land subsidence research has advanced rapidly in recent decades, and integrating InSAR with machine learning has become an important research direction. However, InSAR-derived surface deformation reflects only total deformation and cannot resolve deformation within soil layers at different depths. To address this limitation, we propose a framework that integrates SAR data, stratified deformation ratios from extensometers, and hydrogeological information. By combining Persistent Scatterer Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (PS-InSAR), K-Means clustering, and a Spike-Transformer model, the framework identifies characteristic subsidence zones, estimates stratified deformation, and predicts stratified deformation with high accuracy. Taking the Beijing Plain as a case study, land subsidence is mainly controlled by the second (25.8%) and third (69.79%) compressible layer groups, with maximum subsidence rates of 61 and 83 mm/yr, respectively. Vertically, owing to the spatial heterogeneity of factors such as groundwater-level changes and the lithologic composition of the compressible strata, the dominant subsidence layer varies across the plain: the third compressible layer group dominates in the northeastern plain (Zone 1) and southeastern plain (Zones 4–5), whereas the second compressible layer group dominates in the northwestern plain (Zone 2) and central plain (Zone 3). In addition, the zonal and stratified predictions of the Spike-Transformer model capture variations in deformation rates across different compressible layer groups, with a maximum RMSE of 3.12 mm and MAE of 2.47 mm. This framework provides a transferable approach for zone-specific and stratified management of land subsidence, with important implications for refined subsidence prevention and control.

title: Impact of floods on surface water quality: a systematic review and comprehensive assessment
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Apoorva Bamal, Md Galal Uddin, Reza Ahmadian, Marcelo Gomes Miguez, Agnieszka I. Olbert
abstract: Floods, as extreme flow events, are among the costliest and devastating natural hazards. Among the various domains impacted by flooding, environmental degradation, particularly the deterioration of water quality (WQ), is one of the most impacted yet often overlooked. Therefore, it is essential to understand the nature and source of water pollution associated with flooding. This study aims to evaluate and assess multiple studies conducted globally to determine the impact of floods on WQ. A literature review and assessment of 66 studies published between 2007 and 2026 was conducted using the total comprehensiveness score (TCS). To support the scoring process, studies that scored more than 70% of the maximum achievable TCS (15.4) are considered the most detailed and comprehensive in addressing the objectives of this review. 16 studies achieved a TCS above 15.4, indicating that a limited number of studies incorporate a broader set of factors in this domain. A higher number of studies were conducted post the year 2021, highlighting both scientific progress and a growing focus on WQ impacts from disasters such as floods, beyond the traditionally emphasized socio-economic loss. Among the shortlisted studies, fluvial floods are the most frequently examined, followed by pluvial floods and coastal floods. During fluvial floods, turbidity increased by up to two orders of magnitude, while nutrient concentrations (TN, TP) typically rose by ∼ 10–30%. In contrast, pluvial floods were characterised by dilution-driven decreases in EC and TDS, with DOX, BOD and COD showing variable responses across flood types. This review evaluates flood impacts on WQ, catchment characteristics, and sources of WQ modification. The findings of the research reveal that not all WQ parameters are responsible for WQ degradation during every flood event. Rather, it is a combination of certain parameters that leads to deteriorated WQ. WQ degradation depends on interacting factors such as flood duration, extent, depth, and flow dynamics. In overall, this study provides an overview of the multiple cascading impacts of floods on WQ, along with a detailed perspective on the set of criteria that should be considered in future research.

title: A prompt-conditioned multimodal framework for streamflow prediction with lightweight task adaptation
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Xudong Li, Senchang Hu, Wenyi Zhang, Wuyou Xiao, Wenzhuo Shi, Jiaqi Ruan, Zhao Xu, Hao Wang
abstract: Accurate streamflow prediction is pivotal for water resource management and disaster prevention. However, achieving high-accuracy streamflow prediction remains challenging due to the strong nonlinearity, non-stationarity, and multi-factor coupling of hydrological processes. This study proposes a prompt-conditioned multimodal framework for streamflow prediction with lightweight task adaptation of a frozen pre-trained Transformer backbone, providing a feasible framework for multimodal streamflow prediction. The proposed framework uses Generative Pre-trained Transformer 2 (GPT-2) as a frozen pre-trained backbone. Through trainable multimodal embedding layers and a prediction decoder, historical streamflow, meteorological forcing, statistical and static watershed attributes are mapped into a unified embedding space. Meanwhile, structured textual prompts are used to encode task instructions and static watershed descriptors as contextual conditioning information. Experiments in two sub-basins of the Yangtze River Basin show that the proposed model achieves better overall performance than the evaluated data-driven baselines, including CNN, LSTM, Transformer, and PatchTST, in multi-step forecasting tasks from 1 to 7 days ahead. Zero-shot within-region cross-basin validation between the two sub-basins suggests that the proposed framework can retain reasonable predictive skill without target-basin retraining, achieving an average NSE of 0.69 after updating the target-basin descriptors in the prompt. Ablation experiments suggest that prompt-carried basin/task contextual information and statistical features provide complementary conditioning and scale-related information for the normalized numerical embeddings. Overall, the proposed method provides a feasible prompt-conditioned multimodal framework for streamflow prediction and offers new insights into the development of hydrological models.

title: Hydrological controls on antibiotics and mixture risks in upland and lowland rivers: a dual-tracer study combining antibiotics and DOM optical properties
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Zhaoxin Su, Shuangbing Huang, Fengchun Yang, Jiayi Li, Zhijie Wang, Junwei Zhao
abstract: Understanding how antibiotics behave in upland and lowland rivers draining mixed urban-agricultural catchments is essential for hydrology-driven water quality management. We investigated 48 antibiotics and Dissolved Organic Matter (DOM) optical properties at 49 sites along 12 rivers spanning upland headwaters influenced by urban land use and lowland reaches draining predominantly agricultural plains during dry (low-flow) and wet (high-flow) seasons. By combining antibiotic profiles with DOM fluorescence and absorbance indices, including PARAFAC components, we applied a dual-tracer framework that uses antibiotics together with DOM optical properties to interpret spatial and seasonal patterns under contrasting hydrological and land-use settings. Upland rivers subject to urban point sources showed pronounced dry-season antibiotic concentration peaks, consistent with wastewater-dominated inputs under limited dilution. In contrast, lowland rivers draining intensively cultivated areas exhibited the highest cumulative mixture‑level ecological risks, driven by cocktails of antibiotics transported from both urban and agricultural sources. Protein‑like DOM signals were associated with human-use antibiotics in urban‑influenced upland reaches, whereas humic-like components aligned with veterinary antibiotic dominance in agricultural lowlands, indicating stronger runoff contributions during wet conditions. Overall, our results show that flow regime and land use jointly control the redistribution of antibiotic concentrations and mixture risks across multiple rivers, and demonstrate the value of a dual-tracer approach that combines antibiotics with DOM optical properties to diagnose point- and diffuse-source contributions in mixed-use river catchments.

title: Evaluation of groundwater vulnerability in an alluvial aquifer using FEM-based VES modelling and hydrochemical analysis: a case study from Kasur, Pakistan
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Idrees Khan, Yi-an Cui, Hao Li, Umair Khan, Inayath-Ur-Rahman, Warda Yousaf
abstract: Groundwater degradation in industrial alluvial basins requires integrated assessment. Rapid industrialization and intensive agriculture have degraded groundwater quality, threatening drinking water and public health, especially in semi-arid regions where surface water is limited. In such settings, groundwater degradation has become a recurrent challenge, progressively compromising water potability, yet integrated frameworks for its systematic assessment remain limited. This study integrates geophysical and hydrochemical methods to evaluate aquifer conditions and vulnerability in Kasur, Pakistan. A total of 52 Vertical Electrical Sounding (VES) stations characterized subsurface variability. Finite Element Method (FEM) forward modelling and regularized Levenberg–Marquardt inversion resolved four- and five-layer models with aquifer thicknesses exceeding 210 m. Derived aquifer parameters showed spatial variability, including longitudinal conductance (2.6–14 Ω−1), transverse resistance (728.0–9350 Ω·m2), and hydraulic conductivity (31–69 m/day). The Aquifer Vulnerability Index (AVI) indicates high to extremely high vulnerability. The Groundwater Quality Index (GWQI) ranged from 39.1 to 158.4, revealing a transition from good to unsuitable water quality. High GWQI zones corresponded to elevated EC, TDS, Cl−, and SO4 2− concentrations. These zones spatially coincide with low-resistivity anomalies identified by FEM modelling, with EC (r = 0.980), TDS (r = 0.976), and chloride (r = 0.964) showing the strongest correlations with GWQI. The strong spatial coherence among resistivity distributions, aquifer parameters, AVI classes, and GWQI patterns confirms that industrial effluent infiltration controls groundwater deterioration. This integrated framework provides a robust approach for aquifer vulnerability assessment and supports targeted monitoring and improved effluent management in the Kasur industrial corridor.

title: Genetic programming for modeling water-energy-environment coupled systems: taking the upper Yangtze River basin as an example
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Jun Guo, Taixin Zhang, Chao Wang, Zhongzheng He, Yongqiang Wang, Jiahao Lu, Hui Qin
abstract: Accurate modelling of complex water supply-power generation-environment (WPE) coupled systems remains a critical challenge in hydrological research, with existing methods facing trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and operability. This study proposes a genetic programming (GP)-based modelling approach for WPE-coupled systems, taking the Upper Yangtze River Basin as the study area and using 23 years (1998–2020) of hydrological and socio-economic data. For the first time, we systematically compared the performances of GP, system dynamics (SD), and 10 mainstream data-driven methods under identical small-sample conditions and conducted an ablation analysis to quantify the contributions of periodic and trend operators to the GP model performance. The results show that (1) The SD model exhibits excellent dynamic simulation capabilities (test RMSE = 17.87 for total basin water use, MAPE = 1.07%–19.03%) but requires extensive mechanistic expertise; (2) the proposed GP model achieves comparable accuracy to SD (test RMSE = 6.67–604.38, MAPE = 0.18%–11.09%) while avoiding complex mathematical derivations; (3) deep learning models suffer from severe overfitting under small-sample conditions (LSTM test RMSE up to 15750.97); and (4) the contributions of periodic and trend operators show significant variable specificity with no universal pattern. The GP method balances modelling accuracy and operability, providing a practical alternative for WPE system modelling in data-scarce regions and offering scientific guidance for method selection in watershed management applications.

title: Enhanced identification of watershed hydrological extremes using an improved drought index incorporating hydrological non-stationarity
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Xiaoteng Pang, Jianwei Liu, Qin Zhang, Haihua Jing, Xinghan Xu, Longhai Shen, Jianxu Han
abstract: Hydrological time series increasingly exhibit non-stationary behavior under environmental change, challenging traditional assessments of hydrological regimes that rely on stationarity assumptions. This study develops a GAMLSS–NSRI framework that explicitly incorporates temporal, seasonal, and meteorological drivers to characterize watershed conditions of runoff abundance and deficiency. Nearly 300 model configurations, involving different distribution functions, response-variable transformations, and covariate structures, were systematically evaluated to identify an optimal generalized additive model for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS), which was then used to construct a non-stationary standardized runoff index (NSRI). The framework was applied to the Taoer River Basin (TRB) for validation. Results indicate that (1) response-variable transformation plays a dominant role in improving model performance; (2) the resulting NSRI shows overall verification performance than standardized runoff index (SRI), with higher probability of detection (POD), Heidke skill score (HSS), and AUC under both full-sample and leave-one-out evaluations, while its advantage remains evident when false-alarm diagnostics are considered; and (3) following the runoff regime shift, hydrological controls transition from mean-dominated to variability-dominated processes, increasing the likelihood of abrupt floods and droughts. Overall, the proposed GAMLSS–NSRI framework effectively captures both the risk and driving mechanisms of hydrological extremes, offering a robust basis for flood and drought risk management under non-stationary conditions.

title: Enhancing water management in data-scarce watersheds using satellite and reanalysis precipitation: a combined SWAT+ and SMOGN machine learning approach
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Manuel Almeida, Narciso Ambrósio, Senlin Zhu, Pedro Coelho
abstract: This study addresses a key gap in hydrological modelling: the lack of a robust and integrated methodological framework for reliable streamflow simulation in data-scarce regions. This gap is addressed through the joint evaluation of a physically based model (Soil and Water Assessment Tool Plus, SWAT+) and multiple machine learning models under multiple precipitation datasets and resampling strategies implemented using SMOGN, as well as complementary evaluation frameworks. The approach integrates satellite and reanalysis precipitation products (Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation, MSWEP; Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement, IMERG; and ERA5-Land), and a dual evaluation framework using conventional performance metrics and Flow Duration Curve indicators, enabling a comprehensive assessment of hydrological behaviour across flow regimes. The analysis was conducted in two contrasting Angolan watersheds (2716–94,976 km2) representing temperate and tropical savanna climates. Results show that model performance rankings are sensitive to the choice of evaluation metric, with notable discrepancies between conventional metrics and Flow Duration Curve-based indicators, which better capture hydrological extremes. Across models and watersheds, MSWEP emerges as the most robust precipitation dataset, while ERA5-Land performance is more watershed-dependent and influenced by calibration effects. Importantly, higher agreement with observed rainfall does not necessarily translate into superior hydrological model performance. Overall, both SWAT+ and machine learning models provide reliable streamflow predictions for water management applications. Random Forest and Artificial Neural Network models with no or moderate resampling, together with SWAT+, are recommended for operational use, highlighting the importance of multi-metric evaluation and context-specific modelling strategies.

title: Intelligent mining of generation operation rules for cascade hydropower reservoirs driven by large language models and knowledge graphs
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Zhong-kai Feng, Teng Lin, Wen-jing Niu, Yang Xiao, Tao Yang, Hongwu Tang
abstract: The rapid expansion of cascade hydropower reservoirs in China has introduced significant operational challenges, including high-dimensional parameter coordination, complex constraint coupling, and limited interpretability of traditional operation rules. To address these issues, this study proposes an intelligent framework for mining power generation operation rules by integrating a Large Language Model (LLM) and a Knowledge Graph (KG). The methodology involves three key steps: (1) Leveraging the LLM’s natural language processing capabilities to extract unstructured textual knowledge from reservoir operation literature, which is then structured and stored in a domain-specific KG; (2) Designing a KG-based model incorporating reservoir entities, temporal attributes, operational conditions, and decision actions to enable standardized and computable representation of rules; (3) Formulating an optimization model aimed at maximizing power generation while adhering to flood control and ecological constraints, solved using an enhanced Cooperation Search Algorithm (CSA). A case study of four reservoirs in the lower Jinsha River (Wudongde, Baihetan, Xiluodu, and Xiangjiaba) demonstrates that the proposed CSA outperforms classical algorithms in convergence and optimization efficiency under complex scenarios. The derived rules exhibit high applicability, practicality, and interpretability, supported by the extensible KG-driven knowledge base.

title: Coupling spatial heterogeneity and temporal dynamics in graph neural networks for accurate forecasting of water quality
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Bin Yang, Ruihao Zhou, Junjiang Zhou, Hui Li, Shenglian Luo
abstract: Accurate forecasting of water quality is important for environmental management and government decision-making. Despite that deep learning-based methods have attracted extensive attention in this field, their performance and generalization ability remain challenging due to the inherent spatial heterogeneity and temporal dynamics involved in multi-station and multi-step forecasting. To address this challenge, we proposed a novel deep learning-based model, termed Shifted Spatiotemporal Window Attention-based Graph Neural Network (SGNN), which explicitly couples spatial heterogeneity and temporal dynamics for multi-station and multi-step water quality forecasting. SGNN introduces an adaptive graph constructor to generate an adaptive graph, and a shifted window block which integrates shifted window-attention and shifted window-adaptive graph convolutional network to account for spatial heterogeneity and temporal dynamics. Its performance was evaluated on a real-world dataset collected in the Dongting Lake basin. Experiment results indicate that SGNN outperforms existing models in both multi-station and multi-step forecasting for a wide range of water quality indicators. Take the electrical conductivity for example, SGNN achieves R2 values of 0.9654, 0.9581, 0.9505 and 0.9338 respectively for 4, 12, 24 and 48 h forecasting. Additionally, generalization experiment indicates that SGNN maintained high accuracy for a different time period. These findings indicate SGNN is effective for multi-station and multi-step water quality forecasting, which is useful for environmental management.

title: A stepwise precision improvement framework for urban lake hydrodynamic-water quality numerical models
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Yue Cheng, Yiping Li, Haibin Yan, Yuxuan Zhou, Hongzhe Pan, Yu Cheng, Yang Hu, Chaomin Yang, Heyun Xin, Carlo Gualtieri
abstract: Accurate numerical simulation of hydrodynamics and water quality in urban lakes is fundamental for pollution control, ecological restoration, and evidence-based water management. However, achieving high simulation accuracy remains challenging due to strong anthropogenic regulation, complex boundary conditions, and unstable water quality responses. Based on an input-process-state layered optimization logic, this study proposes a diagnostic-informed and decision-oriented framework for urban lake hydrodynamic-water quality numerical modelling. Oriented by simulation error sources, the framework integrates six core optimization components- topographic data refinement, grid resolution optimization, boundary input optimization, initial condition configuration, parameter uncertainty analysis, and state-variable data assimilation. Unlike conventional calibration-oriented workflows, each component is first used to diagnose whether its associate uncertainty source significantly constrains model performance. The resulting diagnostic information is then translated into targeted modelling decisions and optimization actions. The proposed framework is applied to two typologically distinct urban lakes in the Yangtze River Basin, with contrasting hydrological regulation and pollution characteristics. Quantitative results demonstrated that the marginal effects of each component differ substantially. State-variable data assimilation provided the largest overall improvement, followed by parameter uncertainty analysis and boundary input optimization. Bathymetry refinement and grid optimization mainly improved physical consistency but contributed relatively limited gains to overall predictive accuracy. The effectiveness of data assimilation was strongly dependent on baseline model performance, with larger benefits observed for models exhibiting greater initial errors. By explicitly linking uncertainty diagnosis, modelling decisions, and optimization actions, the proposed framework provided a reproducible and decision-oriented paradigm for urban lake hydrodynamic-water quality modelling.

title: A spatial recursion framework for nonstationary flood frequency analysis considering river network dependence and reservoir routing
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Chengkai Liu, Lihua Xiong, Yanlai Zhou, Jie Chen, Rongrong Li, Hua Chen
abstract: Flood frequency analysis (FFA) is critical for hydraulic design and flood risk management, yet the traditional stationarity assumption is increasingly challenged by climate change and intensive human activities. In large regulated basins, upstream reservoir operations substantially reshape downstream flood regimes. The controlled discharges propagate along the river network and interact with tributary inflows, thereby heightening the complexity of flood dynamics in downstream reaches. Most existing nonstationary flood frequency analysis (NFFA) methods are limited to single-site modeling and rarely provide a unified framework that simultaneously accounts for river network dependence and reservoir flood routing processes. To address this gap, this study proposes a spatial recursive framework for NFFA (SRF-NFFA) that explicitly incorporates river network dependence and reservoir flood routing within a probabilistic structure. The framework integrates GAMLSS-based marginal and conditional models, copula-based dependence structures, and physically based reservoir routing functions, recursively deriving nonstationary flood peak distributions from upstream source nodes to downstream recursive nodes. Nonstationary design floods are further estimated using the equivalent reliability method based on bias-corrected CMIP6 multi-model ensemble precipitation projections. The framework is applied to seven nodes in the Hanjiang River Basin (1964–2020), including three mega reservoirs and four gauging stations. Annual precipitation is introduced as a climatic covariate to characterize the impacts of climate change on flood peaks. Results show that, except for two upstream stations, flood peaks at all other regulated nodes exhibit significant nonstationary behavior. The application of SRF-NFFA in the Hanjiang River Basin confirms its effectiveness in flood frequency estimation across all nodes. In addition, nonstationary design floods are substantially reduced relative to stationary estimates, especially in downstream reaches. Compared with single-site covariate-based NFFA (SS-C-NFFA), although SS-C-NFFA achieves slightly lower fitting errors in conventional goodness-of-fit metrics, SRF-NFFA provides a more physically consistent representation of spatial flood dependence and reduces uncertainty in flood quantile estimates by leveraging reservoir routing processes and river network dependence for regional information sharing. Overall, SRF‑NFFA provides a reliable analytical tool for basin‑scale flood risk management in regulated river systems.

title: Impact of sand mining on groundwater-surface water interactions in the Vietnamese Mekong Delta
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Chengcheng Wu, Edward Park, Dung Duc Tran, Jingyu Wang, Nguyen Le Duy, Grigorios Vasilopoulos, Chengpeng Lu
abstract: Sand mining is a pressing socio-environmental concern in the Vietnamese Mekong Delta (VMD), profoundly reshaping river morphology, sediment transport, and hydrological processes. Although previous research has identified the adverse effects of sand extraction on surface water and channel morphology, its impact on groundwater has never been examined. This study addresses this unexplored relationship by providing the first investigation of how sand mining influences groundwater storage and surface water–groundwater (SW–GW) interactions, using an integrated approach of long-term field observations, remote sensing data, and hydrological records. Spatiotemporal analyses reveal a declining trend in groundwater storage anomalies (GWSA) and groundwater levels (GWLs), particularly in areas of intense mining activity. GWL decline rates in the unconfined aquifers within 1995–2017 vary spatially with a mean decline of 0.03 m/year. The maximum rate of GWL decline is 0.09 m/year and observed at the northeast and the minimum rate is 0.01 m/year and observed at coastal delta. GWSA has declined over 20 years in three phases: a sharp decrease (2002–2006, 3.2 × 107 m3/year), partial recovery (2006–2015, 8 × 106 m3/year), and a slower decline (since 2015, 4 × 106 m3/year). The findings indicate that extensive riverbed incision caused by sand mining deepens channels, disrupts sediment redistribution, and accelerates groundwater depletion while reducing aquifer recharge. As a result, riverbed hydraulic connectivity is weakened, leading to a diminished SW-GW exchange. A conceptual model is proposed to illustrate the mechanisms driving these changes. These insights suggest that regulating sand extraction intensity, monitoring incision hotspots, and integrating sediment management with groundwater governance may help mitigate long-term hydrological degradation in the VMD and similar large deltas.

title: Effects of the spatial distribution of internal water storage on soil–plant hydraulic function
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Vinod Shankar Pathak, Venkatraman Srinivasan
abstract: Plant internal water storage buffers hydraulic disequilibrium between soil water supply and atmospheric demand, yet its contribution remains poorly quantified, especially in roots. Soil-plant-atmosphere continuum (SPAC) models commonly equate root uptake with basal sap flux, neglecting root storage and potentially biasing predictions of diurnal water fluxes and hydraulic stress. Here, we developed a coupled SPAC model that explicitly resolves water storage in root and shoot compartments. The model was evaluated under field atmospheric and soil moisture conditions to quantify the individual and combined roles of root and shoot storage in plant hydraulic function. Our results show that internal storage supplied 51% of early-day transpiration (35.5% shoot, 15.5% root), and removing either compartment reduced transpiration despite compensatory increases in the remaining storage use and root uptake. However, eliminating root and shoot storage individually increased cumulative hydraulic stress by up to 129% and 176%, respectively, relative to the full-storage baseline under critical water potential thresholds. A dry-down analysis showed that reliance on storage use increased by 37% under soil moisture limitation. These results suggest that internal storage is a key regulator of plant hydraulic function and drought stress mitigation. Models that neglect storage in roots or shoot underestimate drought resistance and overpredict hydraulic failure risk, limiting their ability to scale plant hydraulics to ecosystem processes.

title: Precipitation changes dominate the reduced interannual variability of runoff across the Yarlung Tsangpo River Basin
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Zelong Yang, Xiaomang Liu, Kaiwen Wang, Changming Liu
abstract: River runoff from high-mountain basins underpins downstream water resources and hydropower generation, yet it is highly sensitive to climate warming. While the impacts of warming on long-term runoff magnitude are well documented, the evolution of interannual runoff variability—a critical indicator of water supply stability—and causal physical processes remain poorly understood. Bridging this knowledge gap is particularly urgent in the Yarlung Tsangpo River Basin, a typical cryosphere-influenced basin undergoing rapid climate change. Here, we examined annual runoff variations in the Yarlung Tsangpo River and its three tributaries (the Lhasa, Nyang, and Nianchu rivers) from 1982 to 2020. A novel decomposition framework was developed and integrated with a conceptual hydrological model to quantitatively attribute runoff dynamics to individual components: rainfall runoff (Q rain), snowmelt runoff (Q snow), and glacier runoff (Q glacier). Our results demonstrate that annual runoff magnitude has increased across all four rivers, primarily driven by increasing Q rain. The absolute increases are 5.25 km3 (Yarlung Tsangpo River), 0.32 km3 (Lhasa River), 0.97 km3 (Nyang River), and 0.01 km3 (Nianchu River), respectively. Conversely, interannual runoff variability generally decreases, as the reduced interannual variability of Q rain and Q glacier counteracts the enhanced interannual variability of Q snow. An exception is observed in the Lhasa River, where interannual runoff variability increases due to strengthened synchronization between Q rain and Q snow. The relative changes in the coefficient of variation (CV) of runoff are −11.5%, +9.9%, −13.5%, and −4.8% for the four rivers. Process-based analyses reveal that shifts in the interannual variability of Q rain and Q snow mirror the declining interannual rainfall variability and rising interannual snowfall variability, respectively. Meanwhile, the reduced interannual variability of Q glacier is linked to weakened temperature fluctuations and continued glacier shrinkage. These findings advance the understanding of hydrological dynamics in glacier- and snowmelt-influenced basins.

title: Flood frequency analysis combining observed streamflows with simulations from a continental hydrological model
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Julien Lerat, Jai Vaze, Quan J. Wang
abstract: Despite considerable effort to improve Flood Frequency Analysis (FFA) models, FFA remains a highly uncertain endeavour for sites with limited streamflow records. This paper introduces the Covariate-Based Flood Frequency Inference (CoFFI), in which a censored bivariate flood probability distribution is jointly fitted to two annual maxima series: one from a short available observation record and the other from a long simulation generated by a continental hydrological model. CoFFI combines two General Extreme Value (GEV) marginals and a Gumbel-Hougaard copula, with parameters estimated within a Bayesian inference scheme. In terms of predictive uncertainty, CoFFI applied to short record lengths between 10 and 25 years yields predictions as narrow as those of a standard univariate FFA model fitted to twice as many data points. Furthermore, CoFFI yields predictions with smaller discrepancies from long-term FFA curves than a univariate model, with the CoFFI discrepancy equivalent to that of a univariate model using 5 to 10 more years of data. These performance gains decrease for data records longer than 25 years and become negligible at 50 years. Finally, a simple criterion is proposed to anticipate CoFFI performance: the method is considered likely to outperform benchmark models when the Kendall- τ coefficient between observed and simulated annual maxima exceeds 0.4.

title: Determining an optimal sample size range for UAV-assisted satellite soil moisture content retrieval using a farthest point sampling method
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Furong Yang, Ning Geng, Yifei Yao, Rong Liu, Zugui Huang, Shikun Sun, Yadan Du
abstract: Accurate field-scale mapping of Surface Soil Moisture Content (SMC) is essential for precision agriculture and water resources management. While the reliable retrieval of SMC from optical satellite data remains challenging in mixed pixels containing both soil and vegetation, leveraging Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV) has demonstrated significant potential for enhancing satellite-based SMC estimation. Specifically, the integration of UAV multispectral data into the Linear Spectral Reconstruction (LSR) method has enabled large-scale and high-accuracy SMC monitoring. However, achieving high SMC retrieval accuracy using the LSR-like UAV-based satellite enhancement method is constrained by sampling cost. In particular, the lack of an optimized sampling strategy has become one of the most critical limitations for satellite-based SMC retrieval. To address this issue, this study focuses on determining an appropriate sample size range required to ensure stable and accurate SMC retrieval, and proposes a Farthest Point Sampling (FPS) strategy that accounts for spatial representativeness in sampling design. Taking the Baojixia-Jiaokou irrigation district in Shaanxi Province, China, as the study area, the FPS method was compared with conditioned Latin Hypercube Sampling (cLHS), the Random Combination Method (RCM) and Spatially Balanced Sampling (SBS) under different sample sizes within an LSR-enhanced SMC retrieval framework. The results demonstrate that FPS generally provided more stable retrieval performance within a limited sample size range. Specifically, 50–90 samples were recommended as an appropriate sample size range, within which retrieval accuracy remained relatively stable, whereas further increasing the sample size produced only limited marginal improvements or even reduced retrieval stability. These findings systematically reveal the coupled effects of sample size and spatial sampling design on SMC retrieval performance and provide practical, cost-effective guidance for field sampling, thereby facilitating the operational application of UAV-assisted satellite enhancement methods such as LSR in regional SMC monitoring.

title: Environmental modulation of storm–flood response scale in a semi-arid urbanizing basin: a stability-validated power-law modelling
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Yixuan Wang, Tingxi Liu, Ruizhong Gao, Xiaomin Liu, Limin Duan, Ping Miao, Hongli Ma, Shiming Bai
abstract: Environmental change can alter storm-flood response, but whether it modifies the baseline response magnitude or rainfall-response elasticity remains unclear in semi-arid urbanizing basins. This study developed a stability-validated power-law modelling framework to examine event-scale flood peaks in the Ulan Moron River Basin, northern China. Candidate influencing variables were screened using calibration-set tests, validation consistency, and bootstrap stability, and alternative model structures were compared by allowing environmental covariates to affect the scaling parameter (α), the rainfall-response exponents (β and γ), or both. Results showed that maximum 1-h rainfall intensity and total rainfall amount were the dominant storm controls, while environmental effects were more consistently represented through α than through β and γ. The dynamic scaling parameter αt decreased significantly over the study period, indicating a downward shift in baseline storm-flood response magnitude. From the early to late period, combined environmental change was associated with an approximately 69.8% reduction in α, mainly linked to integrated urban hydrological development, with additional contributions from temperature, surface energy partitioning, and vegetation regulation. Fixed-storm scenarios showed that environmental modulation produced the same relative effect across storm magnitudes but larger absolute flood-peak changes under larger storms. These findings suggest that environmental change primarily shifted the flood-response scale rather than producing robust storm-type-dependent changes in rainfall-response elasticity. The inferred effects should be interpreted as conditional, basin-specific associations rather than definitive causal estimates.

title: Transformation dynamics and controlling factors of dissolved organic matter along a groundwater–river–reservoir continuum in a subtropical karst region
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Wen Lai, Xinlu Su, Jia Qin, Peng Chen, Jing Xiao, Qiaoqiao Huan, Tao Zhang, Jianhong Li, Hui Yang, Junbing Pu
abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) represents the dominant pool of organic carbon in aquatic systems and undergoes microbial degradation and photodegradation—processes that govern its fate through CO2 evasion to the atmosphere, long-term sequestration via sedimentary burial, or reconfiguration into distinct DOM molecular fractions. The dynamics of DOM exert a critical influence the carbon balance and water environment of natural aquatic systems. In groundwater–fed rivers, reservoir construction alters natural hydrological regimes, establishing a groundwater–river–reservoir continuum that profoundly modulates DOM transport and transformation. Despite its ecological and biogeochemical significance, current knowledge regarding DOM sources and transformation pathways within such coupled systems remains incomplete. This study focuses on a groundwater–river–reservoir continuum in a subtropical karst area of southern China. By integrating excitation-emission matrix fluorescence spectroscopy (EEMs), PARAFAC modeling and End-member mixing model (EMMA), this study characterized spatiotemporal variations in DOM source and transformation processes across contrasting hydrological and seasonal conditions. Results indicate that allochthonous inputs generally dominated DOM contributions during April (spring), accounting for approximately 50%–60% in flowing-type waters (FTW) area and up to ∼80% in impounding-type waters (ITW) area. In July (summer and rainy season), enhanced biological activity increased the relative importance of autochthonous production, particularly in the FTW area, where its contribution rose to about 40%–50%, while the ITW area remained largely allochthonous-dominated (∼65%–80%). In December (dry season), reduced microbial activity and selective preservation promoted the accumulation of more refractory, humic-rich DOM, with autochthonous contributions becoming more pronounced in the FTW area (∼70%–80%) but remaining comparatively low in the ITW area (∼15%–40%). Reservoir-induced flow attenuation prolonged DOM residence time, while thermal stratification controlled vertical distribution. Collectively, these findings highlight a spatially differentiated yet seasonally coordinated regulation of DOM sources along the continuum. Overall, this study enhances understanding of DOM transformation along the hydrological continuum and provides new insights into the key mechanisms regulating carbon biogeochemical cycling in karst watersheds.

title: Transition pathways of compound heatwave-pluvial extremes in the Pearl River Basin
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Yingying Xu, Zhiyong Liu, Yifan Huang, Chengshuai Liu, Caihong Hu
abstract: As global warming intensifies, compound heatwave-pluvial extremes (CHPEs), defined by the concurrent or temporally connected occurrence of extreme heat and heavy precipitation, pose growing risks to regional hydrological systems. This study investigates CHPEs in the Pearl River Basin, a monsoon dominated region with complex hydroclimatic conditions. An integrated framework is developed that combines grid-based dynamic thresholds, hydroclimatic typology, and multilayer Markov networks to characterize the spatiotemporal evolution and transition dynamics of CHPEs. Results show that extreme temperature and precipitation thresholds exhibit strong spatial heterogeneity and seasonal variability across the basin, reflecting the nonlinear organization of coupled energy-moisture processes. From 1940 to 2024, basin-wide CHPE occurrences display substantial interannual variability but no persistent long-term trend. In contrast, their spatial distribution shows a clear pattern of coastal intensification and inland attenuation, suggesting differentiated regional responses linked to urban heat-island amplification and evolving monsoon moisture transport. Network-based transition analysis further reveals a shift in the structural configuration of CHPE risks, with diffusive precipitation regimes increasingly transitioning toward aggregation-intensification and explosive convective modes. Although transition probabilities vary with spatial scale, the dominant pathways remain robust across scales. These findings improve understanding of CHPE dynamics and support adaptive risk management in complex hydroclimatic regions.

title: Intercomparison of gridded hydroclimate reconstruction datasets in Asia and evaluation of regional hydroclimate changes
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Wenzheng Nie, Dunxian She, Jun Xia, Guizeng Qi
abstract: Gridded hydroclimate reconstructions spanning past centuries are essential for understanding long-term spatiotemporal hydroclimate variability. However, discrepancies among existing datasets—arising from differences in proxy types and reconstruction methods—introduce substantial uncertainty in regional assessments. In this study, we compiled and comprehensively evaluated eight major gridded hydroclimate reconstructions for Asia using instrumental and newly developed proxy data. The intercomparison reveals distinct regional differences in reconstruction skill, reflecting variations in proxy coverage and methodology. Notably, both drought‐ and pluvial‐affected areas have markedly expanded since the 1950 s, marking the onset of intensified hydroclimatic variability across Asia. Further analysis identifies five significant regional hotspots—two drought‐prone and three pluvial‐prone—where the frequency of extreme events has notably increased compared with earlier centuries, indicating a shift toward more variable hydroclimatic conditions in recent decades. These findings highlight strong spatial contrasts in hydroclimate change, providing an essential reference for paleohydroclimate research and the refinement of future gridded reconstructions in Asia.

title: Assessing reservoir water quality using UAV-based multispectral and thermal imagery integrated with machine and deep learning approaches
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Mohammad Sadegh Khodaei, Mohammad Reza Nikoo, Siamak Boudaghpour, Malik Al-Wardy
abstract: Monitoring water quality in reservoirs is critical for municipal water security and agricultural viability. UAV imagery has been widely applied to monitor the spatiotemporal variation of water quality parameters (WQPs) in many inland waters. However, its application over large, featureless aquatic environments has been constrained due to the inherent limitations of conventional photogrammetry in georeferencing imagery. Furthermore, although numerous studies have leveraged multispectral UAV imagery for WQP estimation, the potential of integrating UAV-acquired thermal infrared data to enhance predictive performance remains largely underexplored. In this regard, we adapted a framework for preprocessing and direct georeferencing of UAV imagery over the Wadi Dayqah reservoir, Oman’s largest dam. Six WQPs, namely chlorophyll-a (Chl-a), dissolved oxygen (DO), temperature, electrical conductivity (EC), turbidity, and oxidation–reduction potential (ORP), were estimated using four machine learning models (LR, SVR, RF, XGBoost) and three tabular deep learning algorithms (TabPFN, TabNet, FT-Transformer). Two scenarios were used to estimate WQPs. In the first, multispectral imagery was used, whereas in the second, multispectral data was combined with thermal infrared data. Results showed that TabPFN and TabNet outperformed machine learning algorithms. Additionally, incorporating thermal imagery enhanced the accuracy of WQP estimation, with the best improvements observed for temperature (TabPFN, from R2 = 0.93 to 0.99), DO (TabNet, from R2 = 0.71 to 0.79), and turbidity (TabPFN, from R2 = 0.83 to 0.90), whereas Chl-a estimation showed minor improvements.

title: External terrestrial moisture supplies still dominate the variations in precipitation over the greening Loess Plateau
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Jiahui Du, Ting Hua, Yuanzhu Zhang, Jiajie Xu
abstract: Extensive greening in the Loess Plateau (LP) may have substantially altered the atmospheric water cycle. However, in this area characterized by limited precipitation with high interannual variability, it remains unclear on the role of local evapotranspiration and external terrestrial moisture supplies on the changes in precipitation, which hinders our understanding of local water security and future sustainable development. Therefore, using data from the Water Accounting Model-2layers moisture tracking model, this study analyzed the moisture sources of precipitation and their roles in the interannual variability of precipitation over the LP during 2001–2018. Our results show that precipitation in the LP predominately (69.32%) originates from external terrestrial moisture supplies, and the moisture contribution from the westerlies-dominated regions and Asian summer monsoon regions tend to peak during cold and warm seasons, respectively. Although climatologically the southeastern China (SE China, 18.94%), the Tibetan Plateau (TP, 14.12%), and the LP (9.51%) are major water source regions for precipitation over the LP, their relative roles in regulating the interannual variability are not ranked accordingly: in summer and autumn when most rainfall occurs, the relative contribution of SE China is positively correlated with precipitation variations (r = 0.25 and 0.13, respectively), whereas that of TP has significantly negative correlations (r = -0.57 and −0.46, respectively, both p < 0.1), suggesting that when precipitation increases, its moisture supplies come mainly from the south direction. Moreover, the local recycling ratio is negatively correlated with precipitation, further supporting that changes in precipitation are dominated by external terrestrial moisture supplies and not by changes in local evaporation. Our study offers a mechanism analysis on the atmospheric cycle of Loess Plateau under the implementation of massive ecological restoration projects, which still highlights the importance of large-scale atmospheric circulation for changes in water resources.

title: A flow matching-based deep generative framework for end-to-end hydrogeological parameter inversion in subsurface multiphase flow
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Piyang Liu, Jie Wang, Kai Zhang, Liming Zhang, Jinding Zhang, Zhi Tao, Jun Yao, Wei Zhang
abstract: Hydrogeological parameter inversion is a key component in constructing reliable groundwater-flow and multiphase-flow models, which are essential for geo-environmental applications such as groundwater resource management, subsurface contaminant remediation, and geological CO2 sequestration in deep saline aquifers. Traditional inversion methods usually require numerous forward simulations for iterative parameter updating or calibration, which can lead to a substantial computational burden. This study proposes an end-to-end generative inversion framework based on conditional flow matching, termed the Flow Matching Inversion Methodology (FMIM). Using a rectified-flow linear probability path, FMIM learns a continuous-time mapping from transient dynamic observations to data-conditioned hydrogeological parameter-field realizations. To reduce spatial redundancy in high-dimensional parameter fields, principal component analysis is introduced for parameter compression. An enhanced U-Net architecture with time and observation-condition embedding modules is then used to predict the conditional vector field that guides the ordinary differential equation generation process. The proposed framework is evaluated using four cases: a two-dimensional heterogeneous multiphase displacement aquifer model, the three-dimensional Brugge benchmark, a deep saline aquifer CO2 sequestration model, and a field-scale subsurface fluid extraction case. The results show that FMIM achieves lower parameter-field root mean square error than the tested deep generative baselines and data-matching performance close to that of ESMDA. After offline training, FMIM can efficiently generate multiple observation-conditioned plausible parameter-field realizations with improved data-space agreement after forward simulation. Overall, this study demonstrates that conditional flow matching provides a feasible generative modeling strategy for hydrogeological parameter inversion.

title: Positive matrix factorization for runoff component separation: a paired catchment application
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Eliza Płaczkowska, Alexandra Weber, Larissa Böhrkircher, Niels Döscher, Gunnar Ketzler, Heye R. Bogena, Michael Leuchner
abstract: Total streamflow is composed of two main components: direct runoff and baseflow, which represent different hydrological responses within a catchment. Traditional hydrograph separation methods based only on discharge data usually distinguish between these two end-members. However, both components can include waters with different residence times, flow paths, and geochemical histories, indicating that streamflow may consist of several hydrologically and chemically distinct sources. Chemical-based separation methods allow a more detailed identification of streamflow components, particularly in small headwater catchments where hillslope-stream connectivity increases hydrological complexity. In this study, we applied the Positive Matrix Factorization (PMF) model to water quality data from the experimental Wüstebach catchment in Germany. The model was tested in two neighbouring catchments with similar environmental conditions but different slope water movement patterns. The objective was to identify natural streamflow components and assess whether PMF can resolve multiple end-members beyond the traditional runoff-baseflow framework. PMF identified four end-members in the Wüstebach catchment and five in its tributary, revealing a more complex streamflow structure than commonly assumed. These components showed distinct temporal dynamics, indicating varying dominance under different hydrological conditions and suggesting different flow pathways and storage mechanisms. Overall, the results show that both direct runoff and baseflow consist of several hydrochemically distinct sub-components. The study highlights the sensitivity of PMF to subtle geochemical differences and its potential to improve understanding of streamflow sources and hydrological processes in headwater catchments.

title: Interlayer solution fissure flows as important and stable recharge sources for epikarst springs: evidence from isotopic measurements and in situ observations
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Chunmao Shi, Qiuwen Zhou, Yuan Li, Hang Yang, Ze Yuan, Jian Qiu, Zhanghong Li, Dequan Zhou, Shengtian Yang
abstract: The epikarst is the central hydrological unit of the karst critical zone, playing a crucial role in water storage and transfer. Interlayer solution fissures form a large independent storage zone within the epikarst. Previous research has typically classified interlayer solution fissure flow as a component of conduit and fracture flow, neglecting the regulatory and storage roles of its component in sustaining epikarst springs. Based on in situ observations and isotopic tracers, this study clarifies the contribution of interlayer solution fissure flow to epikarst spring discharge. Results indicate that during the wet season, interlayer solution fissure flow exhibits pronounced vertical differentiation in hydrologic behavior. Shallow horizons exhibit a larger response amplitude to rainfall than deep horizons, yet their water content is markedly lower. Throughout the wet season, interlayer solution fissure flow is characterized by a more enriched δ2H signature (−44.60‰) than vertical conduit flow (−65.80‰) and fracture flow (−63.43‰). Moreover, the hydrologic and isotopic responses of this flow to rainfall are weakened and delayed. Regarding recharge contribution, interlayer solution fissure flow accounts for an average of 27.07% of the total spring discharge, a proportion comparable to that of conduit flow (26.88%) and fracture flow (27.59%). Notably, the contribution of interlayer solution fissures to spring runoff exhibits the widest variability (10.40%–53.30%), indicating that interlayer solution fissure flow is a major source of recharge for epikarst springs. Given its critical role in maintaining the stability of spring discharge, a subhorizontal, slow-flowing interlayer dissolution fissure component for water storage and conveyance should be incorporated into conceptual models of karst aquifers. The findings reported here improve our understanding of the water storage and regulation mechanisms in karst aquifers.

title: Hydraulic reconstruction and geomorphological impacts of surge-induced GLOFs in the Upper Indus Basin
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Saima Ali, Sajid Ali, Lei Wang, Sidra Batool, Xiuping Li, Jharana Nepal
abstract: Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) triggered by glacier surges pose significant hazards to downstream communities in the Upper Indus Basin (UIB), yet their hydraulic characteristics of flood wave propagation and associated geomorphological impacts of these events are poorly quantified. Here, by integrating multi-source remote sensing, two-dimensional (2D) hydraulic modeling (HEC-RAS), and field-based geomorphological assessment, this study reconstructs surge-induced GLOF events from five major surge-type glaciers (Khurdopin, Shishper, Chillingi, Central Rimo, and Chatteboi) in the UIB. Surge dynamics analysis using ITS_LIVE velocity data, terminus advancement and surge history data revealed distinct acceleration patterns with peak surface velocities exceeding 3 km/yr during active phases with Khurdopin recording four distinct GLOF events across separate surge phases between 1989 and 2022. HEC-RAS 2D simulations of validated GLOF events at Shishper (2019) and Khurdopin (2018) demonstrated strong agreement with observed discharge (R = 0.84–0.87, NSE = 0.90–0.93) and moderate-to-high accuracy in reproducing flood discharges and inundation extent (R = 0.69–0.75, NSE = 0.66–0.73). Peak simulated discharges under the high-breach scenario reached 2500 m3/s at Shishper and 2000 m3/s at Khurdopin, with flood waves propagating downstream within 5–6 h.Geomorphological assessment through field surveys and satellite image analysis documented extensive downstream impacts along the Shishper ravine and Shimshal River corridor, including pronounced channel widening, bed scouring, bank erosion, and destruction of critical infrastructure. These findings underscore the urgent need for continuous monitoring of surge-type glaciers and physically-based modeling frameworks to support hazard assessment and early warning system development in glacier-fed mountain basins under a warming climate.

title: Wavelet-Kalman-LSTM fusion: enhancing meteorological drought prediction with robust feature selection and uncertainty quantification
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Akram Seifi, Mumtaz Ali, Hossien Riahi Madvar, Anwar Ali, Mohsin Khan
abstract: Accurate drought forecasting is essential for minimizing socio-economic and environmental impacts but remains challenging due to climatic variability and complexity of droughts. This study presents the Wavelet-Kalman-LSTM (WKLSTM), a new hybrid deep learning framework that combines wavelet decomposition, Kalman filtering, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), improving multi-timescale drought predictions (SPI3, SPI6, SPI9, SPI12) across various regions of Australia. The WKLSTM addresses non-stationarity by decomposing signals into hierarchical subseries using discrete wavelet transforms, denoising coefficients with Kalman filtering, and utilizing LSTM’s temporal modeling. Advanced feature selection techniques such as Boruta, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), and LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) are integrated with eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) to identify critical lagged predictors. The WKLSTM model is assessed against both standalone and hybrid benchmark models, including LSTM, Feedforward Neural Networks (FNN), attention-based LSTM (attLSTM), Convolutional Neural Network combined with Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (CNN-BiGRU), and WLSTM. The results show that the WKLSTM outperforms by achieving R2 values from 0.51 to 0.99 and lowered RMSE by 7% to 33% compared to benchmark models. Monte Carlo simulations quantify uncertainty with 95PPU bounds covering 50–81% of observations, indicating that although WKLSTM performs well across various regions and timescales, high predictive uncertainty persists due to the nonlinear and stochastic nature of droughts. The framework integrates noise reduction, dynamic feature selection, and probabilistic forecasting, enhancing drought prediction, aiding water resource management and climate resilience strategies. This study highlights the effectiveness of WKLSTM in addressing climatic non-linearity and offers practical insights into drought mitigation.

title: Mapping the past: identifying analog precipitation years with reference rainfall metrics
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): M.W. McGauley, R.D. Myers, B.M. Wadzuk
abstract: Stormwater control measures (SCMs) are important for urban climate adaptation and mitigation strategies. Current design approaches use historical rainfall estimates to determine the design case; however these historical rainfall records do not adequately capture the observed nonstationarity resulting from climate change. While there are climate change projections, these have not easily or consistently been brought into practice. There is an opportunity to simulate climate change impacts analytically through analogous observations of other climate regions or past observations, as well as provide a method to express hydrologic observations and model predictions. This study aims to identify past years of rainfall in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA that are analogous to projected precipitation under various climate change scenarios (three socioeconomic pathways projecting three future 25-year periods). Analogous rainfall years were identified using a novel metric that has previously been used to identify reference years of rainfall The analogous years and future projections both indicate the same precipitation risks in the form of larger, extreme events (approximately 10 mm of additional rainfall for the region’s 2-year, 24-hour event on average and preferential selection of the wettest years on record with climate change intensification). However, future temperature projections remain unprecedented in comparison to observations from the analogous precipitation years, where climate change projections consistently indicate a + 2–6 °C anomaly in monthly maximum air temperature from the baseline of 1950–2000 but the analogous years show little to no difference. In all, this work provides the two-fold outcome of a practical means for communicating the risks of climate change with recallable observations, and the potential to indicate observations that could be used in hydrological simulations to model the risks of climate change to water resources systems.

title: Offshore wind farms' impact on phytoplankton carbon and water quality: A multimethod analysis
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Xinglong Guo, Guoqing Li, Hongyuan Shi, Lingrui Guo, Jing Yu
abstract: Offshore wind farms can affect marine ecosystems by altering phytoplankton carbon concentration and water quality. However, most existing studies rely on single observation methods, limiting a comprehensive understanding of these impacts. In this study, field measurements, remote sensing, and numerical simulations were integrated to assess the effects of offshore wind farms on surrounding phytoplankton carbon and water quality, and to explore their relationships. The results showed that (1) the integrated approach effectively captured both large-scale patterns and local dynamic changes in phytoplankton carbon concentration and water quality; (2) offshore wind farms increased phytoplankton carbon and chlorophyll-a concentrations. In summer, the phytoplankton carbon and chlorophyll-a concentrations inside the wind farm were more than twice those outside the wind farm; in winter, the phytoplankton carbon and chlorophyll-a concentrations inside the wind farm were approximately 1.5 and 1.1 times those outside, respectively; (3) dissolved oxygen, inorganic nitrogen, and inorganic phosphorus also increased inside the wind farm. Compared with those outside the wind farm, their increases were 2.93%, 45.72%, and 41.0% in summer, and 1.12%, 39.04%, and 49.59% in winter, respectively. (4) changes in phytoplankton carbon and chlorophyll-a were mainly driven by wind-farm-induced disturbances to the local flow field, rather than by nutrient limitation.

title: Tracing water use sources in rubber monoculture and rubber- Alpinia oxyphylla agroforestry systems using hydrogen and oxygen isotopes
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Weiqing Lin, Bingsun Wu, Jingjing Wang, Yongyi Liang, Zixuan Wang, Zixun Chen, Xiaoyan Lin, Guitong Li, Huichun Ye, Ying Zhang, Jinlong Zhu
abstract: Global climate change has exacerbated the imbalance between water supply and demand worldwide. Large-scale monoculture rubber (Hevea brasiliensis) plantations in tropical regions have profoundly affected regional hydrological processes and soil moisture dynamics. Rubber-Alpinia oxyphylla intercropping systems, have great potential in alleviating these negative effects, however, their water utilization strategies remain poorly understood. In this study, stable isotope compositions (δD and δ18O) of precipitation, soil water, and plant water were monitored in rubber monoculture (RM) and rubber–Alpinia oxyphylla agroforestry (RA) systems from 2021 to 2023. Water sources were first inferred using a direct inference approach, and IsoSource and MixSIAR models were applied to quantify seasonal water uptake patterns. Results showed that precipitation δD and δ18O values (−20.32 ± 18.13‰; −4.05 ± 2.35‰, n = 24) were relatively enriched during the dry season, whereas they were more depleted during the rainy season (−57.68 ± 24.24‰; −7.60 ± 3.18‰, n = 66). δD and δ18O values of atmospheric precipitation exhibited a clear linear relationship (δD = 8.01 δ18O + 5.54, R2 = 0.92). Soil water content (SWC) differed significantly among months, cropping systems, and soil depths (P < 0.001). Qualitative and quantitative analyses indicate that rubber trees primarily absorb shallow soil water during the rainy season, shifting to deeper soil layers in the dry season. In model comparisons, the IsoSource model provides higher accuracy in quantifying plant water sources than the MixSIAR model. Overall, the results provide insights into plant water-use strategies in rubber-based agroforestry systems and may contribute to the optimization of sustainable plantation management in tropical regions.

title: A self-reinforcing feedback loop exacerbates groundwater depletion in semiarid aquifers
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part B Author(s): Younes Fakir, Hamza Sahraoui, Marc Leblanc, Michel Le Page, Sarah Tweed, Hamza Ouatiki, Houssne Bouimouass, Kaoutar Oukaddour, Mohammed Qachar, Abdelghani Chehbouni
abstract: Groundwater depletion is a growing concern in semiarid regions, where aquifer sustainability is increasingly threatened by intensive irrigation. This study investigates the hydrological impacts of depletion on groundwater recharge processes. A multi-faceted approach combining long-term groundwater level analysis, remote sensing-based irrigation water requirements, drought indices, and isotopes (δ18O, 3H) was applied to an alluvial aquifer in central Morocco. Results show a marked acceleration of groundwater depletion post-2000, with decline rates reaching up to 5.8 m/yr in certain sectors, amid expanding irrigation water requirements and droughts. Tritium data reveal a significant reduction in modern recharge in depleted areas where groundwater depths have declined below 50 m, suggesting reduced aquifer renewal. Concurrently, the δ18O values show a transition in the recharge origin from low-altitude local precipitation to high-altitude mountain-derived sources in more depleted zones. A three-component isotopic mixing model confirms that depletion leads to vertical stratification in renewal times and recharge sources, with deeper groundwater that is extensively exploited for irrigation exhibiting older, higher-altitude signatures. The findings indicate that the large thickening of the unsaturated zone, driven by depletion-induced groundwater decline, leads to diminished recharge, creating a reinforcing feedback loop that exacerbates groundwater depletion and complicates aquifer recovery. The results presented here affirm that continued groundwater over-abstraction not only diminishes aquifer storage but also undermines aquifer renewability. Mitigating this unsustainable cycle necessitates immediate interventions to reduce groundwater withdrawals and enhance recharge. Groundwater should be managed as a strategic resource for both human and environmental needs, against climate change impacts, and as a legacy to future generations.

title: Tracing the source and evolution of organic matter in geothermal environments
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Val Maverick Abecia, Andrea Vieth-Hillebrand, Sonia Salah, Ben Laenen, Simona Regenspurg, Valérie Cappuyns
abstract: Despite recent advances in molecular characterization of organic matter in geothermal fluids, its origin, transformation processes, and physicochemical properties remain poorly understood. It can be assumed that dissolved organic matter (DOM) originates from the geothermal reservoir rocks (natural organic matter, NOM) and from anthropogenic additives such as scaling and corrosion inhibitors (synthetic organic matter, Synthetic OM) mixed with the geothermal fluid during operation. In this study, Liquid Chromatography-Organic Carbon Detection (LC-OCD) was used to characterize NOM and Synthetic OM contributions to the geothermal brine. NOM leachability from reservoir rocks was investigated by batch leaching experiments using 3.5 mol L − 1 NaCl at 125 °C and 70 °C.
